title: Well-being is becoming a place-based policy and trust problem rather than a national average
source_unit: OECD Regional Well-Being interactive tool and user guide
geography: OECD regions; the official OECD overview describes comparison across 447 regions, with region definitions and tool versions subject to update

observations.period: Current OECD Regional Well-Being framework; 11 topics

topics.value: income, jobs, housing, health, access to services, environment, education, safety, civic engagement and governance, community, and life satisfaction

beyond_gdp.value: the tool is designed to complement economic statistics with measures of how life is lived in places

policy_route.value: comparable regional measures can help target policy and empower communities to act

observations.method: OECD regional indicator framework combining comparable subnational measures into topic scores and allowing within-country and cross-region comparison.
observations.uncertainty: The dimensions are not a complete account of lived experience; indicator availability, reference years, geographic boundaries, normalization, and the interpretation of topic scores vary by country and update.
observations.subgroup: Residents of metropolitan, intermediate, rural, island, and sparsely populated OECD regions with different service, labor, housing, and institutional conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: A broad well-being dashboard can improve visibility without proving which policy caused an outcome or whether residents experience all dimensions uniformly.

observations.period: Current OECD Regional Well-Being tool; regional comparison coverage

denominator.unit: OECD regions identified in the official tool overview

regional_comparison.value: the tool enables comparison across 447 OECD regions

within_country.value: regions can be compared with one another and with their national context

place_mechanism.value: national averages can conceal materially different combinations of jobs, housing, services, safety, and life satisfaction

observations.method: Interactive place-based comparison using regional indicators and topic scores.
observations.uncertainty: Other OECD pages and newer tool versions display different region counts, indicating a version or boundary-update issue; this record preserves the 447 figure from the primary overview rather than harmonizing incompatible versions.
observations.subgroup: Regions within the same country, including metropolitan and non-metropolitan places that share national institutions but differ in local capacity and exposure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Regional comparison can encourage ranking without explaining migration selection, historic investment, national redistribution, or local governance differences.

observations.period: Regional well-being disparity measurement; within-country comparison

denominator.unit: top and bottom regional quintile groups

disparity_ratio.value: the user guide uses a top-20%-to-bottom-20% comparison to describe within-country regional disparities

distribution.value: regional inequality is not reducible to income because service access, housing, health, safety, education, environment, community, and civic conditions can diverge together or separately

policy_targeting.value: place-based measurement makes it possible to identify where a national improvement is not reaching people or where a local strength could be protected

observations.method: OECD user-guide description of regional well-being scores and top/bottom regional comparison within countries.
observations.uncertainty: A quintile gap is descriptive and sensitive to the number and definition of regions; it does not estimate causal effects, individual inequality, or the distribution within each region.
observations.subgroup: Residents and institutions in high- and low-performing regions, with particular relevance to places experiencing service contraction, weak connectivity, or limited fiscal and administrative capacity.
observations.counterinterpretation: A low regional score may reflect measurement gaps, rural geography, or different preferences as well as material disadvantage; rankings should not substitute for local inquiry.

observations.period: Regional inclusion and governance implications; current OECD framing

regional_gaps.value: regional inequalities extend beyond economic outcomes and often include differences in talent, skills, health, education, and high-speed internet

capacity_route.value: public services, infrastructure, local skills, multi-level governance, and subnational fiscal and strategic capacity are levers for breaking cycles of stagnation

trust_route.value: persistent place-based gaps can become a trust and legitimacy problem when institutions appear unable or unwilling to make local conditions workable

observations.method: Synthesis of the OECD Regional Well-Being framework with OECD inclusion-and-equality-in-regions analysis.
observations.uncertainty: The OECD framing identifies policy levers and associations, not a single causal model linking regional scores to trust, voting, migration, or economic growth.
observations.subgroup: Poorly served rural and peripheral regions, metropolitan regions with stronger service and skills access, local governments, and residents facing uneven opportunity within the same national system.
observations.counterinterpretation: Regional investment alone may not restore trust if residents lack voice, procedural fairness, affordable housing, or confidence that improvements will persist.

related_sources.claim: Official OECD tool overview and 11-topic framework.
Public interactive regional well-being tool and update notes.
OECD framing of regional inequality, service access, and place-based policy capacity.

boundary: This record adds a place-based measurement and policy-targeting route. It does not treat regional scores as individual outcomes, causal policy estimates, a complete measure of lived experience, or proof that regional disparities directly produce political behavior or institutional distrust.
